summary: The HP's purification requirements during Yom Kippur: five full immersions and ten hand-and-foot washings, one immersion for each transition between white linen and golden garments. Each garment change requires a ritual reset through immersion. A tannaitic dispute addresses whether these immersions require the Temple's holy water (kiyor) or whether a regular mikveh is sufficient.

learning.ahaMoment: Five immersions and ten hand-and-foot washings: the HP's body is reset five times across the day, marking each transition between inner (divine presence) and outer (community) service.
learning.memoryAnchor: Five resets: the HP's body is purified five times, matching the five major transitions of his Yom Kippur day.
learning.learnerQuestion: Does the High Priest need a separate immersion for each garment change, or could one immersion at the start of the day suffice for the whole Yom Kippur service?
learning.coreTension: The HP's purity is continuous throughout the day yet each garment change triggers a mandatory ritual reset; the question is whether immersion remedies impurity that has occurred or marks a phase boundary regardless of current purity status.
learning.coreMove: Each garment change marks a distinct service phase with its own sacred character; the immersion is not a remediation of impurity but a ritual demarcation between phases, treating each phase as requiring its own consecrated entry - producing five immersions and ten washings total.

takeaway.text: Each garment change on Yom Kippur requires a separate immersion and hand-and-foot washing regardless of the HP's current purity status, producing five immersions and ten washings for the full day; immersion functions as a phase-boundary consecration, not a response to actual impurity.

learning.learningBlocker: Students assume immersion is only required when impurity has actually occurred; on Yom Kippur, immersion functions as a consecration marker at each phase transition, required even when no impurity has intervened.

learning.ahaMoment: The dispute reflects a fundamental question: does the HP's Yom Kippur immersion require special sanctified water, or is any kosher mikveh water sufficient? The former makes the immersion uniquely Temple-connected; the latter makes it a standard purity act.
learning.memoryAnchor: Holy water vs. regular mikveh: does the HP's immersion require Temple-specific sanctification, or just halachic purity?
learning.learnerQuestion: When the Mishnah prescribes immersion for each garment change, must the HP use the kiyor (the Temple's sacred basin) or does any valid mikveh suffice?
learning.coreTension: If immersion must use the kiyor specifically, the kiyor's limited capacity creates a practical constraint on the service; if any mikveh suffices, the kiyor's special role is diminished.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes between immersions requiring water sanctified in a holy vessel (adjacent to Temple service acts) and those satisfied by an ordinary mikveh, resolving the practical constraint while preserving the kiyor's specific role for particular service transitions.

takeaway.text: Not all five HP immersions on Yom Kippur require the kiyor; the Gemara differentiates between immersions requiring water sanctified in a holy vessel and those satisfied by an ordinary mikveh, preserving the kiyor's specific role without extending it universally.

learning.learningBlocker: Students assume the kiyor is the relevant vessel for all Temple purification and miss that distinct immersion requirements apply to different parts of the Yom Kippur service.

rashiTranslations.en: 'And the garments of the priesthood' - the four white linen garments of the High Priest on Yom Kippur, about which it is written
'and he shall leave them there' (Leviticus 16). 'They are fit for a common priest' - and we hold that the priestly garments
are not subject to misuse of sacred property, since the Torah was not given to ministering angels that they should be
diligent to remove them immediately. 'The broken-necked heifer' - it is written regarding it 'there,' meaning its burial must be there.
'The broken-necked one' - this one and not another. 'Three verses are written' -
[the extra words] 'to you,' 'to atone,' and 'it.' 'One to exclude from notar' -
that if one unwittingly ate blood that had become leftover (notar), one is liable for only one sin,
on account of the blood alone; and likewise if one ate blood of consecrated offerings while in a state of bodily impurity,
which carries karet in all these cases, one is liable for only one sin,
on account of the blood alone; and likewise if one was unwitting regarding the blood but deliberate
regarding one of these other prohibitions, one is exempt from karet
for that other prohibition.
'But regarding piggul one does not need an exclusion' - for if one
ate blood from an offering that became piggul, we derive from another matter entirely
that one is exempt from karet for piggul. 'Whether
for a person or for the altar' - meaning items that others permit,
either for human consumption, such as the meat
of sacred offerings that is eaten, which depends on the tossing of the blood,
since as long as the blood has not been tossed it is forbidden to eat,
as it is written, 'and the blood of your sacrifices shall be poured out' (Deuteronomy 12),
and afterward 'and you shall eat the meat'; or items that permit for the altar,
such as the sacrificial portions, since the tossing of the blood renders them fit
for the altar, as it is written (Leviticus 17), 'and shall dash'
the priest the blood against the altar of the Lord, and afterward
burn the fat as a pleasing aroma' - one is liable
for piggul regarding them: if one eats from
an offering that became piggul, one is liable for karet, as it is written (ibid. 7),
'and the person who eats from it shall bear his iniquity.'
But an item that itself permits others, such as the blood
and the handful, one is not liable for piggul regarding it,
for we derive from peace-offerings that piggul applies specifically to peace-offerings,
since it is peace-offerings that have items permitting the altar
and items permitting a person, for the blood permits
their sacrificial portions for the altar and their meat for eating.
'Mishna: those acts stated' are performed 'in sequence' -
as stated in our Mishna. 'And so too in the Sanctuary' - if he placed some of the sprinklings
on the curtain and the blood spilled, he must bring another bull and begin again the sprinklings
on the curtain, but he need not go back and start over
with the sprinklings on the ark-cover. 'For each is its own separate atonement' -
therefore an atonement that has been completed
remains completed. 'From where he stopped' -
meaning even if that atonement was not completed, he does not need
to go back and give again what he already gave.
'Gemara: within' - meaning in the Holy of Holies. 'In white garments outside' -
such as the casting of lots, the confession, the pouring out
of the remainder of the blood, and all the sprinklings on the curtain and on the golden altar:
if he performed a later act before an earlier one, these do not disqualify it.
But regarding the slaughtering and the scooping of the incense, he concedes that a requirement of the inside is treated like the inside itself.
'In golden garments outside' - such as this ram and the people's ram, if he performed
the removal of the ladle and the fire-pan before them, these do not disqualify it. 'Once a year' -
this shows that where it is written as an indispensable decree, it is written specifically regarding 'once a year.'
'Rabbi' - the daf ends mid-word here; the comment continues on 60b with 'Yehuda holds,' explaining Rabbi Yehuda's view on which acts require the indispensable sequence.
